newsitem.title: FRANCE: France says won't take NATO enlargement hostage.
newsitem.headline: France says won't take NATO enlargement hostage.

text.p: France on Friday repeated its call to offer NATO membership to Romania and Slovenia, but said it would not block the trio of candidates favoured by Washington.

Presidential spokeswoman Catherine Colonna also said Paris did not expect next week's Madrid NATO summit to complete a reform of the alliance's military structure, but remained open to negotiations on its terms for rejoining the integrated command.
U.S. President Bill Clinton has said he will accept only the Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary in the first group of former communist states to be invited to join the alliance in Madrid.

Colonna said nine of the 16 allies favoured adding Romania and Slovenia to the first wave. President Jacques Chirac would "intervene forcefully to explain why all five candidacies are right", she said.
But she added: "It would be inconceivable to take hostage an alliance decision on the three countries on which everyone agrees."
French Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt said earlier: "The enlargement of NATO will be an evolving process."

Clinton told European broadcasters on Thursday: "I don't want to exclude anyone, but I think it quite important on principle that we not admit anyone until we're absolutely sure that their democracy is stable and that they are militarily capable."

Colonna said Chirac would have a private meeting with Clinton in Madrid, probably on Wednesday, but she did not expect the summit to discuss the issue of France's special position outside the allied military structure.
The United States has rejected French demands that it yield NATO's key southern command, which controls the Mediterranean, to a European as part of a new transatlantic balance of power.
"Our conditions are known. They have not changed. We remain available for negotiations," Colonna said.
She said Madrid would be "only a stage" in the renovation of the alliance, and further steps would have to follow.

However, she cited progress in creating a European deputy supreme allied commander who would run operations using NATO assets in which the United States did not participate, calling on a European chain of command within the NATO structure.

Colonna said she expected the summit would also discuss what will happen in Bosnia when the mandate of the NATO-led peace stabilisation force expires in June 1998. France would press for the allies to keep working for stability.

Briefing reporters on the visit of Lithuanian President Algirdas Brazauskas to Paris from next week, Rummelhardt said France considered all European countries which shared NATO's democratic values had a right eventually to join the alliance.
The implication was that Lithuania and other Baltic states too would eventually be entitled to NATO membership.

Russia has adamantly opposed the admission of any former Soviet republics to the western military alliance, warning that such a move would force it to reconsider the "Founding Act" on a cooperative relationship it signed with NATO in May.

Western leaders have said Moscow cannot wield a veto over who joins the alliance, but officials say there is no prospect of NATO admitting the Baltic republics in the foreseeable future and their best hope is eventual European Union membership.
